newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir ghost looms over India-Pakistan talks.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir ghost looms over India-Pakistan talks.

text.p: The disputed region of Kashmir continues to be a thorn in relations between India and Pakistan despite positive gestures made by both sides ahead of a resumption of high-level talks later this week.

Leaders in India's state of Jammu and Kashmir, over which the neighbours have fought two wars since independence from Britain in 1947, said on Tuesday that Kashmir could overshadow other progress in the talks, which resume on Friday after a three-year gap.
Pakistan rules a third of the disputed Himalayan valley of Kashmir and India the rest. Senior diplomats of the two nations are scheduled to meet in New Delhi from March 28 to 31.
"Unless Pakistan stops arming and killing Kashmiris, the talks are useless, an exercise in futility. There can be no peace," Kashmir's revenue minister Abdul Ahad Vakil told Reuters.

Pakistan denies frequent Indian charges of arming guerrillas seeking independence or merger with Pakistan who launched a major offensive against New Delhi in 1990. But Islamabad vocally supports Kashmiri guerrillas in international forums.
No agenda has been announced for the Delhi talks, but Pakistan insists that Kashmir is the "core issue".

Vakil is a senior leader of the ruling National Conference party, which was returned to power in Kashmir in local elections held last October after a nine-year gap in the state, mainly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority province.
"Peace talks and guns cannot go together," Vakil said.
The talks are viewed with equal scepticism by separatist leaders on the other side of Kashmir's political fence.
"We don't oppose talks, but without involving representatives of Kashmir, Indo-Pak dialogue is useless," said Abdul Gani Lone, a spokesman for the umbrella All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference.
The Hurriyat bands some 30 religious and political groups that want a plebiscite in Kashmir for which Pakistan, citing U.N. resolutions, has been campaigning.
Islamabad's campaign received a boost from fellow Moslem countries at a one-day summit meeting of the 54-member Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC) in Islamabad on Sunday.
The OIC declared "our support to the fundamental rights of Kashmiri people, including their right to self-determination".
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have been killed in seven years of bloody violence in the state.

Violence flared at the weekend ahead of the talks. Gunmen killed seven minority Hindus in a village. Four guerrillas and an Indian soldier died in a gunbattle in Srinagar, the state's summer capital. On Monday two leaders of the guerrilla group Tehrik-ul-Mujahideen died in a shootout in central Srinagar.
"The latest violence is only because militants want to show their presence," said an Indian security official who did not want to be identified.

"Dialogue between two neighbouring countries is a welcome step, but when the principal party, Kashmir, is not involved, it will definitely bring no fruits," said a popular Kashmiri separatist leader, Shabir Ahmad Shah.

"Fruitful talks would require the will of two countries to go through a long process of tough negotiations and exhibit a certain amount of flexibility," said Noor Ahmad Baba, political scientist at the University of Kashmir.
